title: PowerShell deep dive for administrators
monthTitle: Automation: PowerShell & Microsoft Graph at Scale
summary: Move beyond one-line commands and learn the object pipeline, parameters, and error model that make PowerShell a real automation language for endpoint operations.
objectives: Explain how PowerShell passes .NET objects through the pipeline rather than text
Write functions with param blocks, typed parameters, and pipeline binding
Use the streams and ErrorAction to control terminating vs non-terminating errors
Filter and shape data efficiently with Where-Object, Select-Object and calculated properties
Choose PowerShell 7 over Windows PowerShell 5.1 and understand the practical differences
Discover and read help for any cmdlet without leaving the console

quiz.q: What flows down the PowerShell pipeline between commands?
options: .NET objects with typed properties and methods
quiz.why: Unlike traditional shells that pipe text, PowerShell passes rich .NET objects, so downstream commands can access properties and methods directly without parsing.

quiz.q: Which parameter forces a non-terminating error to become a terminating one so a try/catch can handle it?
quiz.why: Most cmdlet errors are non-terminating and bypass catch blocks; -ErrorAction Stop promotes them to terminating errors that try/catch can trap.

quiz.q: In a function, which attribute lets a parameter accept values straight from the pipeline?
quiz.why: ValueFromPipeline binds incoming pipeline objects to that parameter, typically processed inside a process{} block for one-at-a-time handling.

quiz.q: Why prefer PowerShell 7 over Windows PowerShell 5.1 for new automation?
options: It is the only version that supports modules
It cannot run old scripts so it is safer
It removes the need for execution policy
It is cross-platform, actively developed, and ships newer language and performance features
quiz.why: PowerShell 7 (built on .NET) is cross-platform and the version that receives new features and fixes; 5.1 is in maintenance only and stays for legacy compatibility.

quiz.q: Name the cmdlet you would run to see the syntax, parameters, and examples for any command.
quiz.answer: Get-Help (for example Get-Help Get-Process -Examples), and Get-Command / Get-Member to discover commands and object members.
quiz.why: Get-Help is the built-in documentation engine; pairing it with Get-Member to inspect object properties is the fastest way to learn an unfamiliar cmdlet.

quiz.q: In one sentence, why is filtering with Where-Object early in a pipeline better than collecting everything first?
quiz.answer: Filtering early reduces the number of objects flowing downstream, which lowers memory use and speeds up the whole pipeline, especially against large device fleets.
quiz.why: Streaming and filtering as close to the source as possible avoids materialising huge collections and is the core habit behind scalable scripts.

body_markdown:
## PowerShell is an object pipeline, not a text shell

If you came from Bash or `cmd`, the biggest mental shift is this: PowerShell pipes **.NET objects**, not text. When you run `Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100`, each process is a full object with properties and methods. You never parse columns by position or count spaces — you ask for the property you want.

```powershell
Get-Process |
    Where-Object { $_.CPU -gt 100 } |
    Sort-Object CPU -Descending |
    Select-Object Name, Id, CPU -First 5
```

The two cmdlets you will lean on forever are **Get-Command** (find things) and **Get-Member** (see what an object actually contains). When you do not know what is on an object, pipe it to `Get-Member`.

## Functions, param blocks, and pipeline binding

Real automation lives in **functions**, not loose one-liners. A function with `[CmdletBinding()]` and a typed `param` block behaves like a built-in cmdlet — it gets `-Verbose`, `-ErrorAction`, and parameter validation for free.

```powershell
function Get-StaleDevice {
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory, ValueFromPipeline)]
        [string]$DeviceName,

        [ValidateRange(1, 365)]
        [int]$StaleAfterDays = 90
    )
    process {
        Write-Verbose "Checking $DeviceName against $StaleAfterDays day window"
        # ... logic per device ...
        [pscustomobject]@{ Device = $DeviceName; StaleAfterDays = $StaleAfterDays }
    }
}
```

The `process{}` block runs once per pipeline object, so the function streams. `ValidateRange` and `ValidateSet` reject bad input before your logic ever runs.

## The error model: terminating vs non-terminating

Most cmdlets emit **non-terminating** errors that print red text but keep going — and crucially, they **slip past `try/catch`**. To trap them you must promote them with **`-ErrorAction Stop`**.

```powershell
try {
    Get-Item 'C:\does-not-exist.txt' -ErrorAction Stop
}
catch {
    Write-Warning "Handled: $($_.Exception.Message)"
}
finally {
    Write-Verbose 'Cleanup runs no matter what'
}
```

PowerShell also has **streams**: success (1), error (2), warning (3), verbose (4), and information (6). Use `Write-Verbose` and `Write-Warning` instead of `Write-Host` so callers can switch detail on and off.

## Shaping data without melting your machine

Against a fleet of thousands of devices, *where* you filter matters. Filter as close to the source as possible so fewer objects travel down the pipeline.

```powershell
Get-ChildItem C:\Logs -Recurse -Filter *.log |
    Where-Object Length -gt 10MB |
    Select-Object FullName,
        @{ Name = 'SizeMB'; Expression = { [math]::Round($_.Length / 1MB, 1) } }
```

The `@{ Name=...; Expression=... }` syntax is a **calculated property** — it lets you rename and transform columns inline.

## PowerShell 7 vs Windows PowerShell 5.1

**Windows PowerShell 5.1** ships in the box and is in maintenance only. **PowerShell 7** is cross-platform, built on modern .NET, faster, and gets all new features — including the Microsoft Graph SDK improvements you will use this month. Install it side by side; it runs as `pwsh`.

```powershell
$PSVersionTable.PSVersion   # confirm which engine you are in
```

## Your task

Write an advanced function `Get-LargeProfile` that accepts computer profile paths from the pipeline, has a `[CmdletBinding()]` block, a mandatory `ValueFromPipeline` path parameter and a validated `-MinSizeMB` threshold (default 5000), uses a `process{}` block, emits a `[pscustomobject]` per oversized profile with a calculated `SizeGB`, and wraps its disk access in a `try/catch` with `-ErrorAction Stop`. Run it with `-Verbose` and confirm the verbose stream appears.

slides.narration: Welcome to Month Two, where we turn you from someone who runs the occasional PowerShell command into someone who writes real automation. This first lesson is the foundation: the object pipeline, functions, the error model, and how to shape data at scale. Get these right and everything else this month becomes easy.

slides.title: Objects, not text
bullets: PowerShell pipes .NET objects, not text lines.
Each object carries typed properties and methods.
No column parsing or counting spaces.
You ask for the property you want by name.
slides.code:
Get-Process |
    Where-Object { $_.CPU -gt 100 } |
    Select-Object Name, Id, CPU -First 5
slides.narration: The single biggest shift coming from Bash or command prompt is this: PowerShell pipes objects, not text. When you run Get dash Process, each process is a full object with properties and methods. You never parse columns by position. You just ask for the property you want, like C P U or Id. Get dash Process piped into Where dash Object piped into Select dash Object reads almost like a sentence.

slides.title: Discover with Get-Command and Get-Member
bullets: Get-Command finds cmdlets by name or noun.
Get-Member shows what an object really contains.
Get-Help gives syntax and examples.
When unsure, pipe to Get-Member.
slides.narration: Two cmdlets will serve you forever. Get dash Command finds things, and Get dash Member shows you what an object actually contains. Whenever you do not know what properties are available, pipe the object into Get dash Member and it tells you. And Get dash Help, especially with dash Examples, is the built-in manual. Learn to read help in the console and you will never be stuck.

slides.title: Functions and param blocks
bullets: Real automation lives in functions, not one-liners.
CmdletBinding makes a function act like a cmdlet.
Typed param blocks validate input up front.
ValidateSet and ValidateRange reject bad input.
slides.narration: Real automation lives in functions, not loose one-liners. When you add the CmdletBinding attribute and a typed param block, your function behaves like a built-in cmdlet. It gets dash Verbose and dash ErrorAction for free. And validation attributes like ValidateRange and ValidateSet reject bad input before your logic ever runs. Notice the mandatory parameter that also accepts values from the pipeline.

slides.title: Pipeline binding and process blocks
bullets: ValueFromPipeline binds incoming objects.
The process block runs once per object.
This makes your function stream, not buffer.
begin and end blocks bookend the run.
slides.narration: When a parameter has ValueFromPipeline, objects coming down the pipe bind to it one at a time. You handle each one inside a process block, which runs once per object. This is what lets your function stream instead of buffering everything in memory. There is also a begin block that runs once at the start, and an end block that runs once at the finish. Use begin to connect, process to work, end to clean up.

slides.title: Terminating vs non-terminating errors
bullets: Most cmdlet errors are non-terminating.
Non-terminating errors slip past try/catch.
ErrorAction Stop promotes them to terminating.
Then catch and finally work as expected.
slides.narration: Here is a trap that catches everyone. Most cmdlet errors are non-terminating. They print red text but keep going, and crucially they slip straight past a try catch block. To actually trap them, you must promote them with dash ErrorAction Stop. Once you do that, your catch block fires and your finally block runs no matter what. Remember this: no ErrorAction Stop, no catch.

slides.title: Streams: stop using Write-Host
bullets: Success, error, warning, verbose, information streams.
Write-Verbose for diagnostics callers can toggle.
Write-Warning for things that need attention.
Write-Host writes to the host, hard to capture.
slides.narration: PowerShell has several output streams: success, error, warning, verbose, and information. Use Write dash Verbose for diagnostic detail that a caller can switch on with dash Verbose, and Write dash Warning for things that need attention. Avoid Write dash Host for logic output, because it writes straight to the screen and is hard to capture or redirect. Streams make your scripts controllable from the outside.

slides.title: Shape data at scale
bullets: Filter close to the source to cut object count.
Fewer objects means less memory, more speed.
Calculated properties rename and transform inline.
Select-Object and Sort-Object finish the shape.

Get-ChildItem C:\Logs -Recurse -Filter *.log |
    Where-Object Length -gt 10MB |

slides.narration: When you run against thousands of devices, where you filter matters enormously. Filter as close to the source as possible so fewer objects travel down the pipeline. That means less memory and a faster script. The calculated property syntax, a hashtable with Name and Expression keys, lets you rename and transform a column inline. Here we turn raw bytes into a tidy size in megabytes.
